labels.og_answer: About 12 m (39 ft) long, roughly 8 to 9 tonnes

top.answer: A large adult Tyrannosaurus rex was about 12 m (39 ft) long, and most were smaller. A large T. rex stood about 3.5 to 4 m (11.5 to 13 ft) high at the hips and came to roughly 8 to 9 tonnes, by bones and body models, an ordinary adult less. Our T. rex, built to SUE's measurements, measures about 11.4 m (37 ft) in this pose, its raised head about 4.6 m (15 ft) up.
top.answer_more: The two largest known T. rex are SUE in Chicago, the longer and more complete skeleton, and Scotty, probably the heavier.

scale.what: Our T. rex beside a person 1.70 m tall, to one scale, built to SUE's measurements. In this pose, head raised and turned, tail swung, it measures about 11.4 m (37 ft). That is more than six and a half people laid end to end. The top of the raised head is about 4.6 m (15 ft) up, and that depends on the pose. Laid out straight the same skeleton would be about 11.8 m (39 ft). SUE's mount in Chicago is about 12 m.

blocks.nav: Which T. rex was the biggest?
blocks.h: Which T. rex was the biggest?
paras: SUE and Scotty are the two largest known T. rex, and each museum calls its animal the largest, each by a different measure. SUE is the longer and by far the more complete skeleton: about 12 m as mounted, about 90 percent by bone volume. Scotty, with the stouter thigh bone, is thought to be the heavier, about 8.9 tonnes by a study of 2019 that a second one backs. The estimates overlap, since SUE's run from about 8.2 to 9.5 tonnes. Nobody knows how big the biggest T. rex that ever lived was. A model of 2024 guesses about 15 tonnes and over 15 m (49 ft), and no such animal has been found.
Three things decide every number on this page.

points: a tape or a computer model runs along the standing skeleton, from the snout to the tip of the tail. SUE's tail end is restored, and every pose changes the number. So we say about 12 m.
The weight from a bone or a body:

with the bone, measure around the thigh bone and apply the rule that links girth to weight in living animals. No living animal on two legs comes near this size, which is the weak point. With a body model, build flesh around the skeleton and multiply volume by density. By the outline chosen, an adult T. rex has come out anywhere from under 6 to over 18 tonnes.
One animal is not the species:

SUE was an old, unusually large animal. Most T. rex stayed smaller, and an ordinary adult sits nearer 5 to 8 tonnes by studies and museums. That is why three numbers stand apart here: our model, SUE and the species.

paras: SUE, found in 1990 in South Dakota and kept in Chicago, is among the most complete big T. rex skeletons. The list follows the skeleton's description of 2003 and is well founded except where marked.

points: The skull, nearly complete, crushed toward the left in the ground.
Both legs, complete down to the ankle, and the right foot nearly whole.
The right arm: upper arm, both forearm bones and parts of the hand.
The sacrum and the hips, the left hip blade broken and pieced together.
Both shoulder blades, the right one with a healed injury.
Parts of every back rib, 26 of about 60 belly ribs (the museum's count), plus the wishbone and an ear bone (both by the museum).
36 tail bones: in 2003, no known T. rex tail was more complete.
The wrist, restored on the mount after other tyrannosaurs.
Almost all of the left foot, of which a single toe bone exists (less sure: the description contradicts itself in one place about which foot is meant).
About 11 of the mount's 47 tail bones, part of them at the tail's end (our sum).
About 34 of some 60 belly ribs, by the museum's count.

end: The skull on the mount is a corrected cast, and the real one stands beside it in its own case.

blocks.intro: For each number: where it came from, and what it means.

rows.text: SUE's mount in Chicago, as the museum gives it and as a computer model of 2011 measured it. The tail end is restored, since 36 of the mount's 47 tail bones were found. So we say about 12 m.

Many sites give this figure. It is Scotty's length, as the news of 2019 put it. The study's summary gives no length, and the museum used to give nearly 12 m. The Natural History Museum in London writes almost 13 m for SUE and Scotty together, with no method named.

The 8.8 is Scotty, 8,870 kg from the girth of its thigh bone, with a wide margin. The 9 is SUE by the Field Museum's 3D model, in US tons, so roughly 8.2 tonnes. The body models of a 2025 study also come close to 9 tonnes. All of them sit inside about 8 to 9 tonnes.

A model of 2024 starts from how many T. rex lived and how they grew. From that it works out how big the biggest might have been: perhaps about 15 tonnes and over 15 m. Nothing of that size has been found, and the authors call such a find extremely unlikely.
That much of SUE was found, but by bone volume, since the missing bones are mostly small. By count it is 250 of about 380, about two thirds.

blocks.intro: For each picture: where it came from, and what we know now.

rows.term: Standing upright like a kangaroo, the tail on the ground
rows.text: The pose of an early skeleton mounted in New York, copied in pictures for decades. We know now that T. rex held its back nearly level and its tail off the ground: the bones of the back were stiff, and the tracks of meat-eating dinosaurs rarely show a dragged tail.

rows.term: Running fast enough to catch a car
rows.text: Older studies and films gave it that speed, but a fast run is out: its legs would have needed far more muscle than they could hold, and running would have overloaded its bones. Most likely it only walked, and a trackway that probably comes from an adult shows just that.

rows.term: Hands turned palms down, with three fingers
rows.text: Often drawn so, but each hand had two fingers. The palms faced each other, says London's Natural History Museum: by the arm bones, no known meat-eating dinosaur could turn its hands palms down.
Films show it, but the two never met. About 80 million years lay between the last Stegosaurus and the first T. rex, more than lie between the last T. rex and us.

paras: Every piece of T. rex skin ever found is scaly. All of it comes from a single animal, Wyrex in Houston: three small patches from the neck, the hips and the base of the tail. The scales are under a millimetre across.

Not one feather has been found on any T. rex, nor on any other large tyrannosaur. Smaller, earlier relatives had thread-like feathers: little Dilong, and Yutyrannus at about 1.4 tonnes, roughly a sixth of SUE. Yutyrannus lived some 60 million years before T. rex. No skin is known from the top of the back, so a thin cover there can be neither shown nor ruled out.
And lips: by a study of 2023, lip and gum most likely covered all the teeth when the mouth was shut. A minority still argues for a crocodile-like face, and no lip has ever been found.

blocks.nav: Why our T. rex looks like this
blocks.h: Why our T. rex looks like this
paras: It is built to the measurements of SUE's bones: thigh bone, upper arm bone, hip blade and skull at their sizes, the rest after another T. rex, rules and our own reconstruction. The colours are ours, because no colour is known for any T. rex. We show the mouth shut from the side, and open closer up, with the band of lip and gum above the upper teeth.

items.q: Was Spinosaurus bigger than T. rex?
items.a: Longer, and most likely lighter. The largest adults were just under 14 m (46 ft) and about 7.4 tonnes, by a model of 2022. That model scales a young skeleton up to the size of the largest snout found. A big T. rex was about 12 m (39 ft) and 8 to 9 tonnes. More on the Spinosaurus page, where both stand to one scale, with its sources.

About 28 years or more, by the growth rings in its bones, as the museum gives it. A study of 2026 puts a T. rex's full size at about 35 to 40 years, so SUE may have been older. It was old in any case, with healed injuries.

paras: Museum of Ages is a digital museum, made by a nonprofit. Free entry, no account. In the animal wing this animal will stand among the others, from the giants of long ago to the last of their kind. The Leonardo da Vinci wing shows what a finished wing looks like.

items.alt: Our seven dinosaurs in a row from the side, to one scale. The longest, our Argentinosaurus, is about 30.6 m (100 ft), two long necks tower over the rest, and a grey person 1.70 m tall looks tiny beside them.
Our megalodon from the side, about 16 m (52 ft) long, mouth closed, dark grey with a paler band along the flank, beside a grey person 1.70 m tall who looks tiny next to it.

Our young Spinosaurus from the side, about 10 m (33 ft) long, with a tall sail and a deep tail. Behind it the pale outline of the largest adults, just under 14 m (46 ft) by a model, and beside it a grey person 1.70 m tall who reaches its hip.
items.line: An adult Spinosaurus was longer than any T. rex found so far, most likely lighter and much lower at the hips. Here our young one stands beside our T. rex, to one scale.

items.alt: Our Brachiosaurus from the side, built at the Chicago skeleton's size, 24.0 m (79 ft) along the backbone, its long neck raised in a gentle curve to a head top 11.5 m (38 ft) up, the neck angle our choice. The front legs are longer than the hind legs, the tail is off the ground, and a grey person 1.70 m tall could walk under its belly.
items.line: Brachiosaurus, a long-necked plant eater of the Late Jurassic, was about 22 to 25 m long and roughly 30 to 45 tonnes, both figures rebuilt from one partial skeleton. Our Brachiosaurus stands beside a person, its head about seven people up in the pose we chose.

items.alt: Our Triceratops from the side, 6.9 m (23 ft) from beak to tail and 2.5 m (8 ft) high over the hips: a wide frill behind the head, two long horns over the eyes, a short one on the nose, four legs. Beside it a grey person 1.70 m tall who reaches about two thirds of the way up its back.
items.line: A big adult Triceratops was about 7 to 8 m long, with a skull about 2 m, longer than SUE's. Our Triceratops stands beside our T. rex to one scale, with what the bones show of the two and what they do not.

items.alt: Our Ankylosaurus from the side, 6.4 m (21 ft) from beak to club, its back 1.7 m (5.6 ft) high over the hips: a low, wide body under rows of bony plates, a broad head carried low, four short legs and a straight tail ending in a flat club. Beside it a grey person 1.70 m tall, as tall as the top of its back.
items.line: Ankylosaurus, an armoured plant eater with a tail club, lived at the same time and in the same land as T. rex and was about 6 to 8 m long. Our Ankylosaurus stands beside our T. rex to one scale, with what the bones show of the two and what they do not.

items.alt: A Stegosaurus from the side: a small low head, two rows of tall plates along the arched back, two of its four tail spikes, the front legs shorter than the hind legs. Beside it a grey person whose head stays below the top of its back.
items.line: The largest Stegosaurus were about 9 m long, and Sophie, the skeleton in London, is about 5.6 m. Our Stegosaurus stands beside our T. rex to one scale, though less time separates T. rex from us than from Stegosaurus.
